bri3d · Oct 24, 2026

Sealing to a reasonable subset of PCRs (ie, not just 7 like the article) is reasonably strong against point-in-time evil maid, no?

Like, in Evil Maid Scenario 1, where the Evil Maid only has one-time access, if you've sealed to say 0,2,4,7,9 , or 7 and 15 with a reasonable setup for what gets extended into 15, the Evil Maid's Fake PIN Entry Software would _not_ validate in the secured boot configuration and couldn't actually unseal the TPM, only coerce you into entering your PIN. Then the Evil Maid would have to physically return to your "correct" boot state with the PIN to unseal the disk, no?

(this is all modulo firmware and early boot exploits, of course, since in that case the attestation could also be forged also)

bubblethink · Oct 24, 2026

What problem is this solving though? The post says they're doing this to avoid typing passphrases. Why would you want the private key hidden in the tpm chip of that device? How will you decrypt if the laptop goes bust or if you move the drive elsewhere?

lakeviewterrace · Oct 24, 2026

The TPM generates a strong, non-exportable key in hardware that is far less susceptible to brute-force attacks.

As opposed to accidentally creating your own key of "4", for instance.

A PIN can be used to protect the TPM from unlocking. Even if you set a PIN of "1234" — it would still be far more secure if the disk and laptop were ever to become separated, because the TPM will have generated a strong key anyway.

The TPM is basically a smart card soldered to the motherboard.

> How will you decrypt if the laptop goes bust or if you move the drive elsewhere

Windows and Apple both generate a recovery key as part of the enrollment process which you can store offline.

hparadiz · Oct 24, 2026

Has nothing to do with distros. This is you encrypting your disk for the kernel to open during boot. It literally prompts you normally when it hits the step where it attempts to mount the main partition. The way Linux does it is far more flexible and secure because the keys aren't sent to some third party and no one can unlock it without your keys. You are free to use anything to sign the LUKS partition besides a TPM or some silly pin like a Yubikey or whatever the hell you want.
